extracted.intended_audience: policy advocates, comment organizers, and rubric designers for administrative rulemaking (notice-and-comment)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating and drafting public comments in administrative rulemaking, with emphasis on how mass comment campaigns are treated and what makes individual comments more likely to receive procedural acknowledgment or substantive influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identical/duplicate comments are discounted
rubrics_metrics.description: A comment that is verbatim identical to thousands of others is functionally counted as one voice (or less). Mass-campaign duplicate text dramatically reduces a comment's effective weight, even where the agency formally counts each submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat exact duplicates as low-effective-weight inputs. Anti-pattern: submitting verbatim form letters at scale and assuming additive influence. Scoring note: lower score for verbatim duplicates; consider de-duplication when tallying unique substantive inputs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personalization or small modifications increase weight
rubrics_metrics.description: Adding even a paragraph of personalized content can lift a comment from the 'mass campaign' category into the 'substantive' category.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage minimal but specific personalization to boost substantive weight: include a personal experience or example; a locally-relevant fact (geography, occupation, family situation); or a specific concern about a specific provision. Scoring: award higher substantive marks to comments with any non-template, original text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Campaigns should be coupled with separately-filed substantive submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: A campaign that produces 100,000 form letters but no separately-filed substantive comment from the sponsoring organization is less effective than a campaign with a strong umbrella comment from the organization plus the form letters as supporting volume.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best practice: the sponsoring organization files an in-depth, separate comment (umbrella/position paper) articulating legal/technical arguments and uses form letters as supporting evidence of broader support. Scoring: treat an organizational umbrella comment as necessary to elevate a campaign's substantive influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mass campaigns receive reduced procedural acknowledgment
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA cites mass campaigns in responses but at lower rates than other comments; procedural acknowledgment (being discussed/cited in response-to-comments documents) is reduced for campaign-style submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the objective is formal acknowledgment in agency response documents, do not rely solely on form letters. Scoring: comments from mass campaigns should be scored lower on expected procedural visibility unless accompanied by substantive, individualized content or organizational filings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Does the comment go beyond verbatim mass-campaign text?
rubrics_metrics.description: Checklist criterion: Does the comment go beyond verbatim mass-campaign text?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete test: compare the comment to known campaign templates; any unique sentences or paragraphs should be noted. Scoring: binary or graded — 'no' for exact matches; 'yes' with degree based on amount of unique content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Includes a personalized experiential or factual element
rubrics_metrics.description: Checklist criterion: Does the comment include a personalized experiential or factual element?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a short anecdote about personal impact, data about local conditions, occupation-related details. Scoring: assign higher weight for first-person experience or verifiable factual detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Localizes the impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Checklist criterion: Does the comment localize the impact (geography, sector, demographic)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Localization strengthens relevance to the rule's expected effects — cite county/city, local industry, demographic group, or specific local conditions. Scoring: higher points for specific local relevance vs. generic national statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accompanied by a separately-filed substantive submission (if part of a campaign)
rubrics_metrics.description: Checklist criterion: If part of a campaign, is it accompanied by a separately-filed substantive submission from the sponsoring organization?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify whether the sponsoring org filed a detailed comment or position document; absence weakens campaign's influence. Scoring: campaigns with an organizational umbrella comment score higher on overall influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identifies at least one specific provision of the proposed rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Checklist criterion: Does the comment identify at least one specific provision of the proposed rule?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strong comments point to specific regulatory text, sections, or provisions and explain how the rule language affects interests. Scoring: award more points to comments that cite precise provisions and explain concrete impacts or suggested changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normative caution: empirical findings are not endorsements of marginalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Cautionary guidance: Balla's findings about procedural discounts should not be read as endorsing the procedural marginalization of mass campaigns; normative arguments (e.g., Mendelson's) that value certain comments remain active.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing rubrics or advising organizers, distinguish between 'what agencies do in practice' and 'what ought to be done normatively.' Nonetheless, empirical reality suggests that substantive personalization produces both procedural acknowledgment and substantive influence; design scoring rubrics to reward personalization while remaining mindful of equity and access concerns.
